slides.1: Today I want to examine the fifth global goal, usually called gender equality. It argues that no opportunity and no ambition should ever depend on whether you were born a boy or a girl.
slides.2: Why should the men in this room really care? Families become stronger and classrooms improve quickly whenever women and girls are doing well. Society advances slowly while half of us is quietly held back.
slides.3: A bird cannot fly when one wing is stronger than the other. Our societies operate similarly, because men and women carry the flight between them. If one half is held down, nobody arrives anywhere.
slides.4: Until recently, most people assumed that a boy would study medicine while his sister stayed at home. Those assumptions still stand like a wall, and they block children from the subjects they really love.
slides.5: This lesson arrives long before anyone mentions a career. Relatives still hand trucks to the boys and dolls to the girls, and children absorb that signal quickly, so imagination narrows early.
slides.6: Around the world, poverty still pulls girls out of the classroom before they have finished. Without reading and writing, decent jobs disappear, and the same shortage returns in the next generation.
slides.7: Consider the pay slip. Women still earn less than men on average, and researchers find that a gap remains even after we compare identical jobs. Money is usually what turns a wish into a decision.
slides.8: Look upwards through almost any large organisation. Men occupy most of the senior positions, while women disappear sharply near the top. People call that barrier the glass ceiling, and it costs everyone better decisions.
slides.9: Housework has never appeared on a payslip. Women still do most of the cleaning, the cooking and the caring, which quietly removes hours from their studies and careers. Shared work gives those hours back.
slides.10: Respect begins with the language that we use about each other. Listen carefully, resist the habit of judging anyone by gender, and never announce that a particular job belongs to boys.
slides.11: At home the change is entirely practical. If boys learn to cook a decent meal and girls learn to repair a bicycle, nobody will grow up completely helpless. Families that share the chores usually argue less.
slides.12: Speaking up is harder than it sounds. If you see a classmate treated badly because of gender, say something anyway, because silence leaves that person completely alone. Small interventions can change a whole school year.
slides.13: Here the news improves. Girls have moved into coding clubs, robotics teams and space projects, because schools have finally started recruiting them, and STEM is where the next discoveries will happen.
slides.14: The internet has opened another door. A girl in a remote village can now follow a whole course on a borrowed tablet, so distance matters far less than it did. Classroom walls have become thinner.
slides.15: Social media has given us thousands of examples. Athletes, artists and leaders now publish their own stories, and millions of teenagers watch them. If you share one of those stories today, the reach grows.
slides.16: Governments have started to act as well. New laws now require equal pay and safer workplaces, because leaders have noticed that economies tend to grow when everyone can work.
slides.17: We have looked at old attitudes, unequal pay and unpaid housework, and we have also seen laws, technology and role models pushing back. Equality is a plan, not a wish.
slides.18: This is my personal promise to you. From today I will support my friends whatever their gender, and I will challenge the usual jokes. Could everybody here decide on one similar promise before tonight?
slides.19: Nobody should expect this to happen overnight. The goals set 2030 as the deadline, and if our whole generation pushes together, we can be far closer than we are today.
slides.20: SDG 5 belongs to everybody in this room. When women and men participate as equals, families, companies and entire countries usually benefit. I have already made my choice, and I hope that you will make yours.
